1.title: Pascal's Principle
1.text:
Pascal's Principle

Pascal's principle states that any change in pressure applied at any point on a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid.

Our big question for this lesson: what principles describe how fluids behave and move? Dive in!

If you've ever dived deep into a pool or lake, you've felt the pressure on your ears. French mathematician and physicist Blaise Pascal found that the pressure at a point in a fluid depends on its depth, not on the shape of the container. He also found that any change in pressure on a confined fluid is passed along, undiminished, to every part of the fluid. That's Pascal's principle.

One great use: hydraulic machines that multiply force. In Figure 10, fluid fills two connected chambers, each with a movable piston of a different area. Push on piston 1 with force F sub 1, and the pressure on the fluid is P sub 1 equals F sub 1 over A sub 1. The fluid pushes on piston 2 with pressure P sub 2 equals F sub 2 over A sub 2.

3.title: The Hydraulic Lift
3.text:
The Hydraulic Lift

The force exerted by the second piston equals F sub 1 times A sub 2 over A sub 1.

By Pascal's principle, the pressure travels through the fluid unchanged, so P sub 2 equals P sub 1. Set F sub 1 over A sub 1 equal to F sub 2 over A sub 2 and solve: F sub 2 equals F sub 1 times A sub 2, divided by A sub 1.

So a small push on a small piston becomes a big push on a big piston. If you push harder on piston 1, F sub 2 grows too, in the same proportion, because the extra pressure is passed along to the big piston, multiplied by its larger area. Dentists' chairs and car lifts at a garage work this way.

4.title: Swimming Under Pressure
4.text:
Swimming Under Pressure

The pressure a column of fluid exerts on a body equals the fluid's density times the column's height times the free-fall acceleration: P equals rho h g.

Dive deeper, and you feel the water pressure grow. That pressure comes from gravity: the weight of all the water above you. More water above, more pressure. Gravity only pulls down, but the fluid passes the pressure in every direction: up, down, and sideways.

Let's build the equation. The pressure is the column's weight, F sub g, over its area, A. The weight is m g, and the mass is the density, rho, times the volume. The volume is the area times the height, A h. So F sub g is rho A h g, and the pressure is rho A h g over A. The areas cancel, leaving P equals rho h g.

So fluid pressure depends only on the fluid's density, the depth, and g. Submersibles like the one in Figure 11 have explored the deepest ocean trenches, where the pressure is more than 1000 times standard air pressure!

5.title: Life at the Hydrothermal Vents
5.text:
Life at the Hydrothermal Vents

Hydrothermal vents form where superheated water flows up from cracks in the seafloor.

Scientists use submersibles to study deep-ocean life. In 1977, the crewed submersible ALVIN found the first hydrothermal vents while cruising over the Pacific Ocean floor. These vents form when superheated water flows up from cracks in the seafloor.

They're thousands of meters down, where the pressure can be over a hundred times standard atmospheric pressure, and sunlight never reaches. Yet they're bursting with life! Giant tube worms carry bacteria in their tissues. The bacteria use hydrogen sulfide from the vent water to make sugar, which powers the whole ecosystem. Fish, mussels, shrimp, clams, and octopuses live there too. Submersibles have since explored vents in the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans.

6.title: Buoyancy
6.text:
Buoyancy

The buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces: F sub buoyant equals rho sub fluid times V times g.

What pushes you up when you swim? Pressure grows with depth, and that creates an upward force called the buoyant force. Compare it to an object's weight, and you can predict whether the object sinks or floats.

Picture a box underwater, with height l and top and bottom area A, so its volume is l A. In Figure 12, the water pushes on every side. The side forces cancel. The force on top is rho h g A, where h is the top's depth. The force on the bottom is rho times the quantity l plus h, times g A, which is bigger. Subtract, and the net upward force is rho l g A, which is rho V g.

That volume is exactly the water the box pushes out of the way, or displaces. So the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid: F sub buoyant equals rho sub fluid times V times g.

7.title: Archimedes' Principle and Sink or Float
7.text:
Archimedes' Principle and Sink or Float

Archimedes' principle states that an object immersed in a fluid has an upward force on it equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

Greek scientist and mathematician Archimedes discovered this in the third century B.C. Archimedes' principle says an immersed object feels an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. The force depends only on the displaced fluid, not on the object's weight.

Let's test three objects in water, each with a volume of 400 cubic centimeters, which is 4.00 times 10 to the negative fourth cubic meters. Water's density is 1.00 times 10 to the third kilograms per cubic meter. The buoyant force on each is 1.00 times 10 to the third kilograms per cubic meter times 4.00 times 10 to the negative fourth cubic meters times 9.8 newtons per kilogram, which is 3.9 newtons.

A 3.60-kilogram steel block weighs 35 newtons, far more than 3.9, so it sinks, though it feels lighter in water than in air. A 0.40-kilogram soda can weighs 3.9 newtons, exactly balanced, so it stays wherever you put it. That's neutral buoyancy. A 0.36-kilogram ice block weighs 3.5 newtons, less than the buoyant force, so it rises. An object floats when its density is less than the fluid's density.

8.title: Example Problem 3, A Granite Block
8.text:
Example Problem 3, A Granite Block

The net force on a submerged object is its weight minus the buoyant force.

A cubic decimeter of granite, 1.00 times 10 to the negative third cubic meters, is submerged in water. Granite's density is 2.70 times 10 to the third kilograms per cubic meter. What's the buoyant force, and what's the net force?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the block with buoyant force up and gravity down. Known: V equals 1.00 times 10 to the negative third cubic meters, rho sub granite equals 2.70 times 10 to the third kilograms per cubic meter, and rho sub water equals 1.00 times 10 to the third kilograms per cubic meter. Unknown: F sub buoyant and F sub net.

Step two: solve. F sub buoyant equals rho sub water V g: 1.00 times 10 to the third kilograms per cubic meter times 1.00 times 10 to the negative third cubic meters times 9.8 newtons per kilogram, which is 9.8 newtons. The weight is rho sub granite V g: 2.70 times 10 to the third times 1.00 times 10 to the negative third times 9.8, which is 26.5 newtons. The net force is 26.5 newtons minus 9.8 newtons, about 17 newtons, downward.

Step three: evaluate. The forces are in newtons. The buoyant force is about one-third of the weight, which makes sense because water is about one-third as dense as granite. It checks out!

testIt.name: Granite block
testIt.how: Swap the block material (1.00 × 10⁻³ m³, submerged in water).

9.title: Ships, Submarines, and Fish
9.text:
Ships, Submarines, and Fish

An object floats when its average density is less than the density of the fluid.

How can a steel ship float? Fold aluminum foil into a little boat, and it floats easily. Add a cargo of pennies, and it rides lower. Crumple it into a tight ball, and it sinks! A hollow boat that's big enough has an average density less than water's. Adding cargo raises that average, so more of the boat sinks below the surface. The crumpled ball is denser than water and sinks.

Submarines pump water into or out of chambers to change their average density, so they can sink or rise. That's how the submersible from the start of the module can rise, sink, or hover: add water to sink, push it out to rise, or balance it for neutral buoyancy. Fish with swim bladders do something similar. Filling the bladder with gas displaces more water and raises the buoyant force, so the fish moves up. Squeezing it smaller lets the fish move down.

testIt.name: Foil boat
testIt.how: Load pennies (2.5 g each) into a foil boat that can displace at most 100 g of water.

10.title: Bernoulli's Principle
10.text:
Bernoulli's Principle

Bernoulli's principle states that as the velocity of a fluid increases, the pressure exerted by that fluid decreases.

Look at the hose in Figure 14. In one photo, water flows out freely. In the other, a thumb narrows the opening, and the water shoots out much faster. The relationship between a moving fluid's speed and its pressure is named for Swiss scientist Daniel Bernoulli. Bernoulli's principle says that as a fluid's velocity increases, the pressure it exerts decreases. It's work and energy conservation, applied to fluids.

You see speedups in streams too, where water rushes through narrow parts of the stream bed. As a channel narrows or widens, the speed changes to keep the overall flow of water the same. Bernoulli's principle also plays a part in your blood pressure, and it helps explain how smoke gets pulled up a chimney.

11.title: Why Faster Means Lower Pressure
11.text:
Why Faster Means Lower Pressure

In a narrowing pipe, fluid speeds up and its pressure drops.

Picture a horizontal pipe full of smoothly flowing ideal fluid. Whatever mass goes in one end must come out the other. Now narrow the pipe, like in Figure 15. To push the same mass through the narrow part in the same time, the fluid must move faster.

Faster fluid has more kinetic energy, so net work must have been done on it. That work comes from the difference between the push moving fluid into the section and the push of fluid out of it. Work depends on force, and force depends on pressure. For the net work to be positive, the pressure at the slow, wide end must be bigger than the pressure at the fast, narrow end.

So, by Bernoulli's principle: when the velocity goes up, the pressure goes down. In Figure 15, v sub 2 is greater than v sub 1, and P sub 2 is less than P sub 1.

testIt.name: Squeezed pipe
testIt.how: Squeeze the middle of a water pipe (wide part: 1.0 m/s at 200 kPa).

12.title: Sprayers and Carburetors
12.text:
Sprayers and Carburetors

Fast-moving fluid creates low pressure that can draw another fluid into the flow.

Bernoulli's principle is everywhere! Paint sprayers use it, and so do hose-end sprayers for spreading fertilizer and pesticides on lawns. In a hose-end sprayer, a strawlike tube dips into the chemical solution. Pull the trigger, and water from the hose rushes past the top of the tube, creating low pressure there. The solution gets pushed up the tube and into the stream.

A gasoline engine's carburetor, where air and gasoline mix, works the same way. In Figure 16, part of it is a tube with a narrow section connected to the fuel supply. The fuel is at the same pressure as the wide part of the tube. The fast air in the narrow part is at lower pressure, so fuel is forced into the airflow. Adjusting the airflow changes how much fuel mixes in. Carburetors are found in older cars and motorcycles and in small machines like lawn mowers.

testIt.name: Carburetor
testIt.how: Speed up air through the carburetor and watch fuel drawn in.

13.title: Streamlines
13.text:
Streamlines

Streamlines are lines representing the flow of fluids around objects.

In everyday talk, to streamline something means to make it simpler or more efficient, like a new system that streamlines signing up for a class. In science, streamlines are lines showing how a fluid flows around an object. Car and airplane makers spend lots of time and money testing designs in wind tunnels, like the car in Figure 17. Objects need less energy to move through smooth, streamlined flow.

Try this in your mind: carefully squeeze tiny drops of food coloring into a smoothly flowing fluid. If the colored lines stay thin and sharp, the flow is streamlined. Where the flow narrows, the lines crowd together, which means faster flow and lower pressure. If the lines swirl and blur, the flow is turbulent, and Bernoulli's principle doesn't apply.

So, what principles describe fluids? Pascal's principle explains how pressure spreads through a confined fluid. P equals rho h g tells how pressure grows with depth. Archimedes' principle predicts sinking and floating. And Bernoulli's principle connects a moving fluid's speed to its pressure.
